title: Accounts Payable
subtitle: Supplier invoices, three-way match, payments and ageing
summary: Accounts Payable answers a vital question for any enterprise: what do we owe suppliers, why do we owe it, and have we paid it correctly? Follow a purchase from supplier invoice through three-way matching, approval, GL posting and bank payment. This is the financial completion of the Procurement and Inventory workflows—and a practical lesson in why every operational action must be connected to trustworthy books.

sections.title: Accounts Payable database architecture · Visual ERD
sections.intro: The financial_ap schema has three business tables and nine declared foreign keys. The AP service links supplier invoices to Procurement, posting journals to the GL, and supplier payments to their invoices.

sections.title: Accounts Payable explained without accounting jargon
paragraphs: The stable manager orders oats. The supplier delivers them. The club has the oats, but the supplier has not yet been paid. Accounts Payable (AP) is the system that keeps track of what the club owes suppliers and when payment is due.

Think of the purchase order as "what we agreed to buy", the goods receipt as "what actually arrived", and the supplier invoice as "what the supplier wants us to pay". Three-way matching compares those three pieces of evidence before authorizing payment.

AP is a sub-ledger: it explains which supplier and which invoice make up the amounts owed. The General Ledger holds the consolidated financial impact; Treasury and the bank handle cash movement and reconciliation.

sections.title: Worked example · 60 ordered, 55 accepted
paragraphs: Imagine Purchasing ordered 60 bags of oats at $20 each, but the receiving team accepted only 55 bags. The order value is $1,200; the accepted inventory value is $1,100. If the supplier invoices all 60 bags, AP should hold or dispute the unmatched $100 rather than silently approve it.

For a correctly matched $1,100 invoice, a simplified inventory flow is: goods receipt Dr Inventory $1,100 / Cr GRNI $1,100; invoice posting Dr GRNI $1,100 / Cr Accounts Payable $1,100; payment Dr Accounts Payable $1,100 / Cr Bank $1,100. The actual posting rules, taxes, price differences and approvals depend on application configuration.

Notice the architectural distinction: receiving stock, establishing a supplier obligation, and moving cash are three different business events. Good ERP design keeps them traceable and independently controlled.

sections.title: The end-to-end Procure-to-Pay story
items: 1. Demand: Inventory identifies low stock and Purchasing raises a requisition.
2. Authorization: A different authorized user approves the purchase order.
3. Receipt: Goods are inspected; only accepted quantity enters Inventory and GRNI is recorded.
4. Invoice: AP captures the supplier bill and matches PO, receipt and invoice.
5. Posting: An approved invoice establishes or reclassifies the payable in the General Ledger.
6. Payment: An authorized payment reduces the supplier balance and the bank balance.
7. Reconciliation: AP ageing and balances are checked against GL control accounts and Treasury bank statements.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Entering an invoice from a PO copies the lines that were received but not yet invoiced. Approval refuses an invoice above the received value plus MATCH_TOLERANCE_PCT, and refuses the person who entered it.
Posting clears GRNI (Dr 2110 / Cr 2100) and books any price variance to 5610 (AP_PRICE_VARIANCE). Expense invoices debit the account on each line.
Payments from a bank account post Dr 2100 / Cr 1100 and appear in Treasury's reconciliation; a reversal restores the balance.
